items.title: Recent trends and analysis in artificial intelligence based detection of triple negative breast cancer
items.abstract: Abstract Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive and heterogeneous breast cancer subtype for which artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across diagnostic, prognostic, and treatment response applications. This study presents a comparative bibliometric analysis of AI-related TNBC research indexed in Scopus (n=1,037), Web of Science (n=557), and PubMed (n=763) from 2013-2026. Publication trends, citation impact, leading contributors, international collaboration, knowledge structure, and thematic evolution were examined using database-appropriate bibliometric and network analyses. Using complete year data through 2025, publication output showed statistically significant increasing trends across all three databases, with 2020-2025 compound annual growth rates of 50.13% for Scopus, 49.78% for Web of Science, and 42.84% for PubMed. The United States emerged as the dominant international collaboration hub, while collaboration between the United States and China formed the strongest bilateral link. Thematic evolution showed an early emphasis on machine learning, followed by expansion of deep learning and radiomics and, more recently, parallel imaging/computational and clinical/biological themes involving MRI, treatment response prediction, the tumor microenvironment, immunotherapy, and precision medicine. Scopus co-citation and bibliographic coupling analyses further identified established intellectual foundations and contemporary research fronts. Overall, AI-TNBC research is expanding rapidly, while data heterogeneity, external validation, interpretability, and clinical translation remain important challenges.

items.title: Reconceptualizing the Role of Elementary School Teachers in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: A Critical Study of Pedagogical Agency, Knowledge Authority, and Educational Ethics
items.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence in primary education is changing the way teaching materials are structured, information is acquired, and learning decisions are made. These changes require a reconsideration of the teacher's position, particularly when system recommendations begin to influence assessments of children's needs and abilities. This article aims to redefine the role of primary school teachers through the relationship between pedagogical agency, knowledge authority, and educational ethics. The review employs a critical narrative literature approach to 19 selected publications from 2021–2026, encompassing empirical research, research reviews, conceptual articles, and policy documents that provide open access or official download facilities. The literature is reviewed based on educational context, type of evidence, conceptual contributions, and limitations of its application to primary schools. The synthesis shows that the benefits of AI depend on learning objectives, professional judgment capacity, and institutional support. Teacher agency requires the authority to review, modify, and reject system recommendations. Knowledge authority rests on the ability to explain the basis for a claim and guide the examination of evidence. Educational ethics need to be embodied in data protection, equitable access, child engagement, and the sharing of responsibilities. The article proposes the role of teachers as learning designers, knowledge assessors, relational facilitators, and advocates for children's interests. This reconceptualization requires case-based professional development and school governance that does not center all technological risks on teachers.

items.title: Regenerative Habitation Collection
items.abstract: Aeon Mundi is a collection of adaptive furnishings and robotic tools designed to connect small-plot, rotational food growing with the everyday life of homes, civic buildings, and shared public spaces. Its six pieces support a connected journey from cultivation and habitat care to harvesting, processing, and transport. Workstations, companion seating, and autonomous carts combine adjustable ergonomics with robotic assistance for moving crops, trays, and tools, keeping people involved at each stage. A common material language unites the collection: polished solid-cast mycelium in natural, vegetable-pigmented hues; sustainably loomed bamboo upholstery; rounded, repairable forms; and fine luminescent accents that respond to work phases. Embedded spatial displays offer abstract, user-invoked cues. Together, these elements frame food production as an accessible part of shared daily life and propose a design system for exploring how productive landscapes and human-centered technology can coexist.

items.title: Rembrandt through the eyes of the machine: Toward explainable Human–AI collaboration in painting attribution
items.abstract: With questions that persist for centuries, art attribution is a complex detective effort that shapes cultural identity. Our goal is to complement human expertise, providing statistical and visual arguments that shed new light on discussions about great masters like Rembrandt and beyond, with long-term implications for art analysis and human–AI collaboration. We present an AI-driven explainable approach to assist painting attribution with up to 97.9% recall, 95.8% accuracy when highly confident, and methods that identify the most relevant areas. This work supports human–AI collaboration by incorporating expert guidance, expanding the outputs with explainable visualizations, tailoring settings to users’ needs, thorough calibrations to avoid overconfidence, and building a dataset that balances quality with quantity and focuses on comparable artists like a master’s pupils and teachers.

items.abstract: Governments are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to deliver services, process cases and inform policy, but the success of these initiatives depends less on the technology than on the capabilities of the public workforce that must use, oversee and explain it. Evidence on how AI reshapes tasks suggests that routine cognitive work is most exposed, while demand grows for analytical, interpersonal and ethical judgement. Yet research on public-sector AI has concentrated on technology adoption and governance, and far less on the reskilling and leadership needed to make adoption work. This paper addresses that gap through an integrative review of literature from public administration, labour economics, leadership and learning science, supplemented by policy sources. The review identifies three capability clusters that AI-enabled public administration requires: digital-technical capability, human-relational capability and adaptive leadership capability. It also finds that evidence-based learning designs, particularly spaced, retrieval-based microlearning embedded in work, offer a scalable route to building these capabilities across large civil services. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and transformational leadership theory, the paper proposes the AI-Ready Public Workforce Capability Framework, which links institutional enablers, capability clusters and learning architecture to public value outcomes. Four propositions and practical recommendations are offered for public managers and training institutions, with reference to India’s Mission Karmayogi.

items.title: Reskilling for AI Adoption: Predicting Workforce Readiness Using Learning Analytics
items.abstract: Organisations adopting artificial intelligence must reskill large parts of their workforce, and the success of reskilling is usually measured by course completion, which says little about whether employees can actually work with AI tools. This paper examines whether learning analytics, the behavioural traces of how employees engage with reskilling, can predict workforce readiness, defined as demonstrated capability to use AI in the job, and how readiness predictions should direct support. A simulation of 3,000 employees generates readiness from a process in which practice, completion, assessment, peer interaction, prior digital skill and recency all contribute, with practice and completion interacting. A gradient-boosting model on the full set of learning-analytics features attains an AUC of 0.75, against 0.68 for completion and assessment scores alone. Practice sessions (0.09) and module completion (0.08) are the strongest predictors, with assessment scores (0.04) and prior digital skill (0.04) secondary. A targeting simulation shows that directing a fixed support budget to employees with marginal predicted readiness raises overall readiness by 4.5 points, against 3.1 points for random allocation. The paper argues that reskilling should be managed on practice and application rather than completion, that readiness predictions should direct support toward employees near the threshold, and that learning analytics should be governed as employee data with developmental purpose.

items.title: Respiratory health effects of occupational biomass smoke exposure among cook cum helpers in rural Assam school kitchens using propensity score matching
items.abstract: The use of biomass fuel in households has many adverse health effects and the use of such fuel in cooking environments as an occupational exposure setting remain unexplored. This study aims to examine the extent of respiratory health risks, as a consequence of exposure to biomass fuel smoke, of cook-cum-helpers of the Mid-Day Meal scheme in rural Assam, India. We utilized a comparative cross sectional study design to investigate 130 cook-cum-helpers from 28 government schools (65 from firewood kitchens and 65 from LPG kitchens). The respiratory symptoms of participants were documented using the standard American Thoracic Society (ATS) questionnaire and pulmonary function tests were conducted using spirometry. Based on the confounders of household biomass exposure and passive smoking, propensity score matching was employed. The Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATET) approach was used and matched regression models were computed in the presence of cluster standard school level errors. The mixed effects and cluster adjusted models were used to conduct sensitivity analyses. Of the matched study population ( n = 116) firewood exposure was found to increase the probability of reporting at least one respiratory symptom by 28.4% points (95% CI 15.6–41.2) and airway obstruction by 22.1% points (95% CI 8.4–35.8). Those firewood exposed workers experienced a 13.95% point greater decline in the mean FEV₁ percent-predicted. A significant exposure–duration gradient (p-trend < 0.001) was found that supports the increase in respiratory health risks with longer durations of employment. These findings were valid across different specifications. Institutional school kitchens that utilize biomass fuel are an occupational health hazard that has and continues to remain underestimated. These findings underscore the need to improve occupational health policies and accelerate the use of clean cooking fuels. However, the cross-sectional design of the study limits causal analysis.

items.title: Responsible Data and AI Practices in Engineering Education: Preparing Graduates for Digital Transformation in Industrial Processes
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools become increasingly integrated into higher education, understanding how engineering students perceive and apply principles of academic integrity, data integrity and responsible AI use has become increasingly important. OBJECTIVES: This study investigates how master’s engineering students perceive and apply principles of academic integrity, data integrity, and responsible AI use. It also explores the potential relevance of these practices for the development of competencies associated with participation in data-driven and AI-enabled professional environments. METHODS: A mixed-methods approach was employed using the PEDRA questionnaire (Perceptions on Ethics and Development of Responsibility in Academia), developed by the authors. The instrument was designed to explore students’ perceptions, experiences, and ethical reasoning regarding academic integrity and responsible research practices. The analysis focused on two questionnaire items addressing the influence of academic honesty on data use and the frequency of AI tool use in academic activities. The study involved master’s engineering students from two higher education institutions. RESULTS: Based on the 48 complete responses analysed, the findings indicate awareness of data integrity principles, particularly regarding anonymity, confidentiality, informed consent, and rigorous data analysis. Ethical referencing and transparency in data handling were mentioned less frequently, suggesting areas for further educational support. Regarding AI adoption, 21 of 48 respondents (43.8%) reported occasional use of AI tools, reflecting a cautious and exploratory approach. Descriptive differences in AI use were observed across age and gender groups, with female respondents being more likely to explore AI while maintaining ethical awareness, although these findings should be interpreted with caution. CONCLUSION: The study highlights the importance of integrating responsible data and AI practices into engineering education. The results suggest that developing students’ capacity to use data and AI critically, transparently, and ethically may support the development of competencies associated with responsible participation in increasingly digital and AI-enabled environments. The PEDRA questionnaire demonstrates potential as an exploratory and diagnostic instrument for identifying educational needs related to academic integrity, responsible AI use, data integrity, and trustworthy digital practice.

items.title: Retroalimentación con IA generativa en la evaluación inclusiva: Marco de mediación docente basado en el diseño universal para el aprendizaje
items.abstract: The incorporation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into educational feedback offers opportunities to expand personalisation and accessibility, but it also raises risks of bias, opacity and the erosion of teacher mediation. The objective of this theoretical-conceptual article was to propose a framework to guide the use of generative AI in feedback from the standpoint of inclusive assessment and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). As method, a selective narrative review of the literature on inclusive assessment, formative feedback and AI in education was conducted across three strands, which were then integrated into a framework of teacher decisions and transversal criteria, contrasted with related models and complemented by a focused search of recent studies on trust and evaluative judgement. As a result, the framework links four teacher decisions (what is assessed, how evidence is gathered, how feedback is given, and what opportunities for improvement are offered) with three transversal quality criteria: accessibility, agency and dialogue, and equity with data protection. It is complemented by a four-level scale of teacher mediation that distinguishes lower- and higher-risk uses, a checklist for reviewing AI-supported feedback before it reaches students, three illustrative examples, and five testable propositions to guide empirical validation. The implications of the framework for teaching practice and institutional policy are discussed, along with its tensions (efficiency versus dialogicity, personalisation versus privacy, linguistic diversity, and the access gap) and its methodological limitations. The article concludes that inclusion does not depend on the tool but on the pedagogical and ethical decisions that govern its use, and that teacher responsibility for interpreting evidence remains irreplaceable.

items.title: Risk-Adaptive Visual Attention Mechanisms Under Dynamic Lane Change Risk: Evidence from a Naturalistic Eye-Tracking Field Study
items.abstract: Understanding drivers’ visual attention adaptation under dynamic lane change risk supports human-centric interaction design. We synchronized eye-tracking metrics, vehicle motion logs, and front-view videos from 36 professional drivers in a naturalistic field experiment. A computer vision-based framework was proposed to extract surrounding vehicle kinematics from monocular footage, and a Modified Lane Change Risk Index was developed to quantify dynamic risk. Results reveal directional heterogeneity, with right lane changes involving conservative scanning and significantly prolonged fixations on the initial lane compared with leftward maneuvers. As risk escalated, drivers prioritized safety-critical areas, with increased saccade frequency and shortened fixation durations. In high-risk right lane changes, the Near Lane Line served as a visual anchor for trajectory correction. High-risk states persisted from execution into stabilization, while drivers tended to lock their gaze on the target lane and neglect side mirror checks. These findings inform risk-adaptive human-machine interfaces and human-centric co-driving systems.

items.abstract: Study Protocol This study protocol presents a reproducible framework for a retrospective secondary analysis of real-world hospital encounters involving patients with diabetes. The proposed research uses the publicly available Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, containing 101,766 historical hospital encounters recorded between 1999 and 2008. The study aims to develop and evaluate a risk-stratified prioritization approach for potential patient follow-up under hypothetical healthcare service-capacity constraints. The planned methodology includes data preprocessing, prediction of observed 30-day hospital readmission, comparison of prioritization strategies, and exploratory assessment of equity-related performance. No observed effects of war, crisis-related service disruption, or clinical interventions are claimed. Capacity-constrained scenarios are hypothetical. Data source: UCI Machine Learning Repository. items.title: Role of Communities of Practice in Technology Leadership Development
items.abstract: This chapter examines the critical role of communities of practice in developing technology leadership capabilities within higher education. Drawing from participant interviews, institutional case studies, and the authors’ direct experiences, we analyze how formal and informal communities shape professional development and organizational innovation. We present detailed examples of successful communities of practice ranging from institutional programs like Dartmouth LEADS and Harvard’s ABCD Committee to cross-institutional collaboratives including the Ivy+ Classroom and Learning Space Technologies (CLST) group and the HAIL Storm network. Our analysis reveals that effective communities of practice share three essential elements: a clearly defined domain of knowledge, an established community of engaged participants, and commitment to evolving shared practices. Key success factors include appropriate group size balancing intimacy with inclusivity, sustainable leadership structures, institutional support for participation, and adaptable meeting formats. The research demonstrates that communities of practice provide critical benefits including peer learning opportunities, professional network development, benchmarking capabilities, and collaborative problem-solving resources – particularly valuable during periods of technological disruption like the emergence of generative AI. For technology leaders, strategic engagement with communities of practice offers pathways for personal development, team enhancement, and organizational advancement. The chapter concludes with practical recommendations for identifying, participating in, and fostering communities of practice as essential leadership development tools in rapidly evolving technological landscapes.

items.title: Safe by Benchmark, Unsafe in Practice: Lessons from 1331 Child-Related AI Incidents
items.abstract: AI systems are increasingly present in children's everyday environments: education, entertainment, social networks, and toys. Their safety is typically assessed at the model level, through benchmarks, red-teaming, and content filtering. However, most AI harm taxonomies lack child-specific evidence and under-specify developmental harm and the stakeholder asymmetries unique to minors. Building on prior taxonomies, we construct a child-centered harm taxonomy mapped to sociotechnical failure modes. We curate and code 1331 publicly reported child-related AI incidents, annotating internal and external harm types and the failure mode implicated in each incident. Our analysis reveals which harms are most prevalent in public reporting, how individual-level and population-level harms relate, and which failures are most often coded alongside harm. We find that harm concentrates in representational, dignity-related, and psychological categories, and co-occurs most often with deployment-context, governance, and misuse failures rather than model defects. Harm to an individual child is also frequently linked to population-level harm, reaching children who never interacted with the system. These findings suggest that model-level evaluations, while necessary, cannot by themselves anticipate the harm pathways most often documented for children. items.title: Self-distillation and antisymmetric constraints enable accurate prediction of protein stability changes from single mutations
items.abstract: Abstract Accurately predicting protein stability changes upon residue-level mutations is essential for protein engineering and design. However, previous computational methods are typically designed for specific tasks and struggle to generalize across different stability systems, preventing the accurate guidance of protein mutagenesis. Sequence-based methods are easier to apply to large-scale protein datasets since they do not rely on high-quality structures. However, existing sequence-based approaches struggle to capture structural changes, resulting in lower performance compared to structure-based methods. In this study, we pro-pose DeepTherm, a sequence-based deep learning solution to model changes in folding free energy (∆∆G) and melting temperature (∆Tm) resulting from single-point mutations. DeepTherm transfers a protein large language model as a core component and incorporates a cross-attention mechanism to capture the contact-map changes around mutated positions. To address data imbalance and the antisymmetric nature of mutation effects, DeepTherm employs a self-distillation inference strategy under the supervision of an antisymmetric constraint. Benchmarking across multiple datasets shows that DeepTherm achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in both ∆∆G and ∆Tm predictions. Furthermore, practical evaluations confirm DeepTherm's capability in accurately ranking protein stability on large-scale datasets and effectively identifying critical structural contacts impacting stability. Detailed analysis on cDNA display proteolysis data further highlights the critical importance of self-distillation and antisymmetric constraints in enhancing predictive performance.

items.title: ServeSmart: Bridging Theory and Practice in Customer Service Education through AI-Supported Experiential Learning
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in higher education to support experiential learning in customer service training, where applying theoretical frameworks such as the SERVQUAL model can be challenging. Students frequently struggle with emotional recognition, immediate decision-making, and applying SERVQUAL dimensions during role-play. To address these gaps, this study introduces ServeSmart, an AI-supported learning system that provides real-time guidance during customer service scenario role-play. Using a preliminary exploratory quantitative survey design, this study evaluated students' perceived learning experiences and the platform's usability. Using a non-probability purposive sampling strategy, 30 undergraduate students participated in individual scenario-based simulations followed by a validated post-evaluation questionnaire. Baseline findings indicated that a majority of participants had difficulty with emotional recognition and lacked immediate instructional feedback during simulations. Post-simulation results revealed that all participants reported higher perceived confidence in executing customer service tasks, a clearer perceived understanding of SERVQUAL concepts, and strong interest in future platform utilization. Overall, the findings demonstrate positive student perceptions of ServeSmart as a supportive experiential learning tool, highlighting its potential to offer an immediate instructional platform in service management education.

items.title: Sex-based Differences in Haematological Parameters Among Fuel Station Workers in Port Harcourt, Nigeria
items.abstract: Petroleum stations, also known as filling stations or gas stations, primarily distribute diesel fuel and gasoline to motor vehicles while simultaneously releasing gases and vapours that contribute to various forms of environmental pollution. This study investigated sex-based variations in blood parameters among forecourt attendants in Port Harcourt, Nigeria. This research was structured as a comparative cross-sectional study utilising randomised sampling techniques. A total of 100 participants, including 50 fuel station workers and 50 non-fuel station workers as controls, were enrolled. Key parameters such as white blood cell count, haemoglobin concentration and biochemical markers were analysed to assess the impact of occupational exposure to petroleum vapours. The data collected in this study were expressed as Mean ± Standard Deviation and analysed using SPSS version 23. Results indicated that while most haematological parameters showed no significant gender differences, females exhibited notably lower haemoglobin (p= <0.0001) and packed cell volume (p= 0.001) compared to males, suggesting a higher vulnerability to the hematotoxic effects of fuel exposure. Additionally, significant deviations in absolute lymphocyte counts (p= 0.024) were observed, indicating potential immunological implications for female workers. The findings underscore the necessity for targeted health interventions and regular monitoring to mitigate health risks associated with prolonged exposure to petroleum products. It is crucial to implement preventive measures, including regular health screenings, nutritional support and improved workplace safety protocols. These interventions will be essential in safeguarding the health of fuel station workers and addressing the occupational health disparities identified in this study.

items.title: Skin Disease Classification Using Convolutional Neural Networks and an Exploratory Approach
items.abstract: The most common and fatal type of cancer worldwide is skin cancer. Prompt treatment and improved patient results rely on the prompt finding and accurate labeling of skin lesions. As deep learning and artificial intelligence progress, automated diagnostic systems have demonstrated encouraging outcomes, especially when developed using extensive dermatological images. This chapter proposed CNN architecture for skin lesions classification utilizing the HAM10000 (“Human Against Machine with 10000 training images”) dataset. 10,015 dermatoscopic pictures collected from diverse demographics and imaging modalities are included in the HAM10000 collection. It includes seven clinically important categories of pigmented skin lesions: Melanocytic nevi (nv): harmless mole-like growths, Melanoma (mel): a severe and aggressive type of skin cancer, Benign keratosis-like lesions (bkl): which comprise seborrheic keratoses and solar lentigines, The most common types of skin cancer are basal cell carcinoma (bcc), actinic keratoses, and intraepithelial carcinoma (akiec): pre-cancerous and early-stage cancerous lesions, Vascular lesions (vasc): which encompass angiomas and haemorrhages, and Dermatofibroma (df): non-cancerous skin nodules. To enhance model performance and ensure data quality, preprocessing methods like Gaussian filtering followed by Grab-Cut segmentation to extract affected area, and data augmentation are utilized for class imbalance issue. The Proposed CNN used to extract the feature; finally soft max classifier is used to classify 7 types of skin disease with validation accuracy of 98.67. This chapter also highlight various CNN Architecture and discuss challenges in recent skin disease classification.

items.title: Smarter Smiles: Revolutionizing Paediatric Dentistry with Artificial Intelligence – A Review
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming paediatric dentistry by supporting dentists in diagnosis, treatment planning, behaviour management, and patient education. AI-based technologies such as machine learning and deep learning enable accurate interpretation of dental images, early detection of caries, prediction of eruption patterns, and identification of developmental anomalies. In addition, AI powered mobile applications, virtual assistants, and chatbots improve communication, reduce dental anxiety, and enhance oral health education among children and parents. These digital tools help personalise care while reducing clinical workload and improving efficiency. This review highlights the evolution of AI in paediatric dentistry, its key applications across behavioural management, diagnostics, forensic identification, and patient communication, as well as its benefits, challenges, and future potential in improving child centred dental care.

items.title: Social physics of cybersecurity
items.abstract: Cybersecurity is increasingly recognised as a complex adaptive socio-technical system in which security outcomes emerge from the interactions of attackers, defenders, users, organisations, regulators, and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents. These interactions generate adaptive feedback loops, strategic behaviour, information diffusion, and network effects that drive the evolution of cyber threats and defences. Consequently, phenomena such as attack propagation, cyber-risk contagion, cascading failures, and systemic resilience cannot be fully understood through static or purely technical perspectives. Although evolutionary game theory (EGT), complex systems science, network science, behavioural research, and cyber economics have each provided valuable insights, the literature remains fragmented, with no unified perspective for explaining cybersecurity as an evolving socio-technical ecosystem. This review develops the concept of Social Physics of Cybersecurity as an interdisciplinary perspective that brings these approaches together with human-AI interaction to explain how collective security outcomes emerge from adaptive interactions within interconnected cyber ecosystems. We synthesise research on attacker-defender co-evolution, finite and structured population dynamics, cyber contagion, critical transitions, systemic cyber risk, and the growing role of AI-enabled multi-agent systems. Building on these perspectives, we propose a unified multilevel view of cybersecurity that links individual strategic behaviour, network-level interactions, and system-wide resilience. We argue that cybersecurity should be understood as a social-physical phenomenon in which resilience and vulnerability emerge from the collective dynamics of interacting human and artificial agents. Finally, we identify key research opportunities for developing empirically grounded, data-driven, and AI-enabled models capable of predicting, analysing, and governing increasingly interconnected and autonomous cyber ecosystems.

items.title: Solving needs or hiding desires? A qualitative study of AI-Powered sex robots in disability services
items.abstract: Individuals with intellectual disabilities face entrenched systemic and cultural barriers to sexual expression, often exacerbated in Chinese contexts by values of ‘face’ and ‘familism’. While artificial intelligence and humanoid sex robots emerge as potential interventions, their ethical and practical viability within disability services remains contested. This study employed Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to explore the perspectives of 12 Chinese social workers regarding the integration of AI-powered intimate technologies. Findings reveal four major themes: systemic barriers to romantic agency, the perceived benefits of ‘risk-free’ simulated intimacy, ethical concerns regarding relational authenticity, and societal reflections on the ‘eternal child’ syndrome. Practitioners recognised robots as tools to bypass parental opposition and institutional liability by eliminating risks of pregnancy and exploitation. However, a critical tension emerged: whether these technologies genuinely empower users or serve as a ‘techno-fix’ to hide disabled sexuality from the neurotypical public. The results highlight a ‘double standard of readiness’, where cognitive competence is used to gatekeep human rights. We argue for a multidisciplinary governance framework that prioritises ‘techno-social’ literacy and challenges the sexual ableism inherent in current service models.

items.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding
items.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

items.title: Sovereign Agency under Physical Constraint: A Critical Review and Quantitative Augmentation of Game-Theoretic and Infrastructure-Centric Models of National AI Compute Ecosystems
items.abstract: Sovereign artificial intelligence has moved from a legal debate about data residency to a practical question of agency across the whole computational value chain: energy, connectivity, data centres, compute, data, models, applications, skills and governance. This paper reviews an AI-generated report that models national compute ecosystems through infrastructure economics, low-precision arithmetic, game theory and Monte Carlo risk analysis, and augments it into a verified academic treatment. Each empirical claim in the source was checked against institutional sources. Several were confirmed: the scale of the CNAS Sovereign AI Index, the UK Council for Science and Technology's definition of sovereignty as agency, the European AI Gigafactories call and its deadline changes, Bangladesh's draft National AI Policy 2026–2030, the OECD's 2026 due diligence guidance and the specifications of current rack-scale systems. Others were corrected, notably the infrastructure share of projects and the temporary nature of a mid-2026 suspension of foreign access to frontier models; unverifiable figures were removed. The augmentation adds three computed analyses. A synthetic quantisation experiment shows why block-scaled 4-bit formats are central to doing more with scarce national compute. A corrected analysis of the source's openness model shows that its optimum is a single planner's choice, not a Nash equilibrium, and derives its comparative statics. A Monte Carlo schedule model shows that headline probabilities of infrastructure delay depend entirely on assumed distributions and should be reported with them. The paper closes with implications for capital-constrained states, with Bangladesh as a reference case, framed at the level of strategy and policy.

items.title: Space Matters: Leading Organizational Change with Innovative Learning Environments
items.abstract: Many institutions have come to recognize the importance of designing physical and digital learning environments based on what we know about how students learn. While higher education can support active learning anywhere, choice architecture suggests that where we learn has a significant impact on how we learn. This chapter will focus on a 25-year retrospective case analysis of leading change with developing physical and digital learning environments at a research-intensive university, through multiple educational disruptions. Adaptations to these changes are structured using change frameworks from the literature to distill four key areas. First, “developing a collaborative vision, governance, and strategic planning” moved opportunistic events to a structured vision. “Decisions based on pedagogical principles, diversity and inclusion” focused on student success and what research has demonstrated can enable successful learning to guide decisions. “Create comprehensive sustainable support” enables a shift of thinking on emerging technologies to look at pedagogical innovation for the long term. Lastly, a “focus on data driven decision making” avoids anecdotal change to support decisions based on actual evidence. This chapter will look toward the future and how learning environments continue to contribute to future teaching and learning success as we adapt to a new disruption bringing us into the age of artificial intelligence (AI). We conclude with recommendations for leaders and centers for teaching and learning (CTLs) on planning physical and digital learning environments and preparing for the next wave of disruption.

items.title: Status and influencing factors of artificial intelligence readiness among nursing students
items.abstract: Objective To investigate the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) readiness among nursing students and analyze its influencing factors, providing evidence for the cultivation of AI literacy in nursing education. Methods A total of 684 nursing students from two universities in Hubei Province were recruited as study participants. Data were collected using a general demographic questionnaire and the Chinese version of the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (C-MAIRS-MS). Descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis were employed for data processing. Results The overall mean score of AI readiness among nursing students was 3.47 ± 0.31; the cognitive dimension scored the highest (3.57 ± 0.44), while the competency dimension scored the lowest (3.32 ± 0.48). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that education level, Self-rated academic performance, Student cadre, Innovation and entrepreneurship project, Large language model use frequency, AI course learning, Programming foundation were significant predictors of AI readiness, collectively explaining 33.3% of the total variance (R 2 = 0.333, adjusted R 2 = 0.311, F = 15.030, P < 0.001) Conclusion Nursing students’ AI readiness remains suboptimal with room for improvement. Targeted interventions addressing key predictors are essential to strengthen AI competency among nursing students.

items.title: Strategi Guru dalam Meningkatkan Kedisiplinan Menghafal Al-Qur’an pada Siswa Program Tahfiz Kelas VIII di MTS Assa’adah II Bungah Gresik
items.abstract: Discipline in memorizing the Qur’an is an important aspect of the tahfiz program because students are required to be consistent in memorizing, reviewing, and maintaining their memorization. In its implementation, students have different levels of motivation, memorization ability, and readiness to submit their memorization. Some students are still reluctant to submit their memorization, lack focus during learning activities, or experience difficulties in maintaining consistency. Therefore, teacher strategies are needed to support students in developing discipline in memorizing the Qur’an. This study aims to describe the strategies applied by teachers to improve discipline in Qur’an memorization among eighth-grade students in the tahfiz program at MTs Assa’adah II Bungah Gresik, the impact of these strategies, and the supporting and inhibiting factors in their implementation. This research employed a qualitative approach with a descriptive research design. Data were collected through observation, interviews, and documentation. The data were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles and Huberman through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that teachers applied strategies including setting memorization targets according to students’ abilities, habituating muroja’ah, providing examples, and giving motivation and guidance to students. The strategies had an impact on students’ discipline in maintaining memorization, conducting muroja’ah, managing their time, and achieving memorization targets. Supporting factors included a conducive learning environment, students’ intrinsic motivation, parental support, and teacher guidance and motivation. Inhibiting factors included fluctuating student motivation, differences in memorization abilities, lack of readiness for memorization submission, and distractions during learning activities. These findings indicate that teacher strategies play a role in supporting the development of students’ discipline and consistency in Qur’an memorization.

items.title: Strategic foresight in the age of AI: Cultivating Futures Literacy among EAP/ESP practitioners
items.abstract: Language education, particularly English for Academic/Specific Purposes (EAP/ESP), is navigating a period of systemic disruption. The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence, arriving just after the significant upheaval of the COVID-19 pandemic, has once again altered institutional policies and reshaped student needs. This continuous flux leaves many practitioners in a state of constant reactivity. In line with the conference theme, Innovations in Language Education: Advancing Pedagogy, Practice and Research, we argue for a shift away from responding to educational change toward anticipating and influencing it. This paper presents the conceptual framework and insights gleaned from participants in a Futures Workshop conducted at the conference. Drawing on the multidisciplinary field of Futures Studies (FS), the workshop introduced language educators to three foundational foresight methodologies: Metaphors, the Futures Triangle, and Scenario Planning. Contextualised within the English as a Medium of Instruction environment of Hong Kong, the paper outlines the theoretical rationale for applying FS to strategic thinking within language education, details the workshop's design, and presents initial participant perspectives on the field's trajectory. We conclude that equipping educators with Futures Literacy is critical for cultivating teacher agency, enabling us to design and advocate for preferable pedagogical futures.

items.title: Structured generative AI preparation and classroom belonging in a six-class randomized trial
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support independent preparation without necessarily strengthening students’ connections to the classroom. We examined a structured instructional protocol combining AI exploration, confidence reflection, unresolved question generation, and instructor responsiveness. Following baseline assessment, six intact undergraduate class sections at one Chinese university were randomized equally, with three sections and 110 students assigned to each condition. Assessments were conducted in Weeks 1, 6, and 12, and the intervention began in Week 2. Recomputed item means were analyzed using equally weighted section-level contrasts with four degrees of freedom, supplemented by exact randomization tests. At Week 12, the between-condition difference in classroom belonging change was 0.361 (95% CI 0.145 to 0.576; Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.029). The corresponding differences were 0.282 for emotional engagement, − 0.497 for reactance to teacher guidance, and − 15.24 points for the confidence–performance discrepancy index (CPDI). Exact two-sided randomization p values were 0.100 for all primary contrasts, the minimum attainable with six balanced sections. Exploratory individual-level pathway and effect-modification analyses were treated as hypothesis-generating because only six sections were observed and the pathway estimates were sensitive to measurement timing. Overall, the structured protocol showed promising differences in classroom belonging and related outcomes, but inference remains limited by the small number of randomized sections, parametric model assumptions, and the preliminary discrepancy measure. The findings therefore concern the combined instructional protocol rather than an isolated effect of GenAI or an established psychological mechanism.

items.title: Structured human resource development with AI support is associated with higher expert rated recruitment task quality among education graduates
items.abstract: Abstract Graduate employability programmes are usually evaluated with self-report measures. We compared a structured human resource development programme supported by generative AI with career guidance matched on topics, duration and facilitator contact. Twelve intact cohorts of graduates seeking education-sector posts in Guangdong, China (N = 186), were allocated as whole units, six per condition, crossed with institution, facilitator and schedule. Blinded experts gave a global rating (0–100) of recruitment-task materials produced on site, under invigilation and without AI, before and after the programme. Ratings were made without a pre-specified rubric, which limits their interpretation. Among 168 participants with post-test data (overall attrition 9.7%), the adjusted difference favoured the AI-supported programme by 5.38 points (95% CI 2.76 to 8.01; d = 0.60) and was stable across eight specifications. Four new self-report scales showed smaller differences (d = 0.12 to 0.29), none significant after Holm correction; each scale could detect only differences of about d = 0.4. The effect on expert ratings exceeded the mean effect on self-report by 0.37 standard deviations (95% CI 0.10 to 0.63). Component analyses were exploratory. The design cannot separate the contribution of AI from structured practice and feedback.

items.title: Structuring evidence in air pollution and cognitive impairment research using a role-analysis framework built on LLM-based entity extraction
items.abstract: Rapid growth in biomedical literature has increased the need for auditable methods that convert article-level text into structured evidence data. Air pollution is increasingly framed as a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline and dementia, but publication growth alone does not indicate a structurally diverse evidence base. We aimed to develop and apply a human-validated large language model (LLM)-assisted role-analysis framework based on structured entity extraction to characterize recent air pollution–cognition evidence. Operationally, role-analysis retains pollutant and cognition-related entities as multi-label fields while assigning a single predominant study-level analytical role to each domain. We conducted an abstract-level evidence-structure analysis of PubMed-indexed human original studies published from 1 January 2020 through 22 March 2026. PubMed formed the primary analytic corpus, and Web of Science was used as a supplementary coverage check. A predefined coding schema was used to extract pollutants, cognitive outcomes, study designs, statistical methods, populations, data sources, geographic settings, and analytical roles from titles and abstracts. LLM-assisted screening, extraction, and role coding were constrained by field definitions, conservative coding rules, and consistency checks. Human validation evaluated screening, extraction, and role-coding outputs. Of the 1,061 PubMed records that entered the four-domain eligibility screening, 406 eligible studies were included. In the screening-validation sample ( n = 106), precision was 1.000, recall was 0.881, accuracy was 0.953, F1 score was 0.937, and Cohen’s κ was 0.899. In the structured-extraction and role-coding validation sample ( n = 81), field-level agreement ranged from 0.765 to 1.000; agreement was 0.926 for pollutant roles and 0.901 for cognition roles. The structured evidence dataset showed concentration around particulate matter and gaseous pollutants, older-adult populations, and cognitive outcomes including global cognitive performance, domain-specific cognition, and dementia-related outcomes. Direct pollutant exposure–cognitive outcome analyses dominated the role structure, whereas mediation, effect modification, and alternative role configurations were uncommon. Evidence sparsity reflected overlapping limitations in pollutant characterization, cognitive domain coverage, analytical role diversity, population representation, geographic distribution, and data-source dependence. The post-2020 air pollution–cognition literature is volume-rich but structurally uneven. A human-validated LLM-assisted role-analysis framework can convert biomedical abstracts into auditable evidence data that preserve multi-label study entities together with study-level analytical-role summaries and help distinguish growth in study volume from structural diversity of the evidence base.

items.title: Sustainable nutrition: integrating food systems, environmental science, and diet to advance public and planetary health
items.abstract: Nutrition science has traditionally focused on dietary intake, nutrient metabolism, physiology, and health outcomes. Although these domains remain fundamental, advancing public health increasingly requires understanding nutrition within the broader systems that shape food production, processing, access, consumption, and environmental sustainability. This Perspective proposes sustainable nutrition as a unifying concept: maintaining nutritional status that supports growth, development, and health across the lifespan while accounting for population needs, context, and the capacity and resilience of food systems. We describe a Nutritional Ecology framework that conceptualizes nutrition as the product of dynamic, reciprocal interactions among human biology, dietary patterns, food systems, and environmental conditions. Agricultural practices affect food quantity, quality, nutrient composition, biodiversity, water resources, greenhouse gas emissions, and ecosystem resilience, while environmental change influences crop productivity, nutrient density, food safety, and nutrition security. Dietary patterns simultaneously affect chronic disease risk and the environmental footprint of food systems. These interdependencies argue against evaluating human health and environmental sustainability in isolation. We therefore call for a transformation toward integrated, systems-based nutrition research that incorporates biological variability, environmental drivers, and system-level interactions. Multidisciplinary collaborations spanning nutrition, food, agricultural, environmental, epidemiologic, computational, systems, and implementation sciences will be essential. Emerging approaches, including systems mapping, network analysis, computational modeling, artificial intelligence, and multiscale data integration, can identify trade-offs and leverage points for intervention. Integrating nutrition, food systems, and environmental science is a scientific necessity for generating evidence across diverse population contexts that supports resilient food systems, effective dietary guidance, improved clinical care, healthier people, and a healthier planet.

items.title: SUSTAINABLESIGHT: a resource-aware vision–edge AI architecture for adaptive navigation and STEM accessibility
items.abstract: Assistive artificial intelligence systems for visually impaired users commonly address mobility and educational accessibility as separate computational tasks, resulting in fragmented architecture, redundant inference, and inefficient use of computational resources. This study presents SUSTAINABLESIGHT, a resource-aware vision–edge AI architecture intended for wearable deployment that integrates navigation perception and mathematical-expression recognition through shared, context-aware execution. The proposed architecture supports navigation (NAV), learning (LEARN), and hybrid (HYBRID) operating modes and employs a mode-aware scheduler to activate only the computational components required by the current task. A reproducible computational evaluation was conducted using public datasets and measured inference traces on a GPU runtime; no physical wearable device was evaluated. For navigation perception, YOLOv8n evaluated on the COCO 2017 validation set achieved a precision of 0.6343, recall of 0.4746, mAP@50 of 0.5188, and mAP@50–95 of 0.3681, with a mean inference latency of 7.24 ms on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU. Mathematical-expression recognition using pix2tex was evaluated on a fixed 500-expression subset of an Im2LaTeX validation dataset; 499 expressions were evaluable, with a mean normalized similarity of 0.5940, median similarity of 0.6394, and median character error rate of 0.4343. The substantially greater computational cost of mathematical recognition motivated adaptive branch activation. In a 1,000-request trace-driven workload, SUSTAINABLESIGHT maintained 100% request coverage while reducing model invocations from 2,000 to 1,098 (45.10%) and mean request latency from 3562.22 ms to 1311.32 ms (63.19%) relative to a fixed unified baseline. Mean-latency reductions of 16.15–81.61% were observed across five workload compositions, and scheduler ablation showed that avoiding unnecessary mathematical-recognition inference accounts for most of the latency improvement. items.title: Systematic Profiling of Encoder Architectures and Multimodal Embeddings in Protein Foundation Models Reveals Data Set-Driven Separability Regimes in Prediction of Allosteric and Orthosteric Binding Sites
items.abstract: Abstract Allosteric regulation represents a fundamental mechanism of protein function, yet distinguishing allosteric from orthosteric protein-binding sites remains a persistent computational challenge. While multimodal protein foundation models offer the potential to integrate complementary biological signals, including sequence, structure, functional annotations, and conformational dynamics, their performance determinants in allosteric binding site detection remain poorly understood. We introduce a unified computational framework for profiling multimodal protein foundation models across distinct binding site separability regimes. Rather than evaluating models solely by predictive accuracy, the framework combines systematic modality embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition to characterize how evolutionary, structural, functional, and dynamical information contributes to allosteric site discrimination. Using the OneProt multimodal model, we evaluate two complementary levels of multimodal integration: (a) encoder architectures that differ in the modalities incorporated during pretraining and (b) downstream combinations of pocket, sequence, and text embeddings used for classification. To systematically probe the determinants of model performance, we benchmark these configurations across four assembled data sets of protein complexes representing a spectrum of biological complexity and a range of structural, dynamic, and evolutionary contexts for orthosteric and allosteric binding sites. Through comprehensive embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition, we demonstrate that model performance is governed primarily by intrinsic data set properties rather than architectural complexity, with data set identity accounting for 63.7% of explainable variance. Across the data sets examined, we identify substantial differences not only in overall separability but also in the information accessible from different pretrained representations. Single-modality controls show that high predictive performance does not necessarily imply reliance on the explicitly provided pocket representation: depending on data set composition, substantial discrimination can already be obtained from sequence- or text-based multimodal representations. Within-protein comparisons nevertheless demonstrate that pocket-containing representations retain binding site-specific discriminatory information when protein identity and the associated sequence and text representations are held constant. At the encoder level, structural and molecular dynamics encoders provide the greatest benefit in intermediate and high separability settings. Example-level analysis further shows that combining data sets can reshape which binding sites are preferentially recognized. These findings establish that the success of multimodal foundation models depends critically on alignment between available modalities and the biological signatures that distinguish regulatory classes in each data set.

items.title: Systematic Scoring Differences in Large Language Model–Based Clinical Benchmarking Reveal Evaluator-Dependent Divergence: Controlled Evaluation Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Large language model (LLM) benchmarking in clinical medicine is increasingly reliant on LLM-based assessment frameworks; in these systems, one AI scores the outputs of another. This practice relies on the assumptions of evaluator neutrality and rubric consistency. These assumptions have not been empirically tested in clinical fields. Objective In this study, we aim to directly examine these assumptions by using the PARM (Planning-Action-Reflection-Memory) framework as a theoretical lens to characterize endovascular device selection and clinical reflective reasoning as a clinical field. Methods We developed a scoring rubric (C1-C6) with 40 clinical vignettes and 6 criteria across 5 endovascular fields (peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic venous insufficiency, coronary in-stent restenosis [ISR], and cerebrovascular/neuroendovascular; 8 vignettes per field). Four LLMs were evaluated as clinical decision support systems: GPT-4o (M1), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (M2), Gemini 1.5 Pro (M3), and Llama 3.3 70B (M4). Two LLMs served as independent raters with the same evaluation criteria: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (rater 1) and GPT-4o (rater 2). The rater identity was intentionally disclosed; the primary research question concerned rater scoring behavior rather than the absolute performance of the model. Human assessment was intentionally excluded because its inclusion would have shifted the study question from rater disagreement to rater accuracy, a distinct and secondary question. Interrater reliability was measured using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC 2,1) two-way random effects modeling. Results The combined ICC(2,1) was 0.153 (95% CI 0.007‐0.295). In this exploratory study, the low ICC was not distributed randomly: the magnitude of score differences varied across models (M2 Δ=+5, M4 Δ=+31, M1 Δ=−46, and M3 Δ=−158 points). Scoring behavior analysis identified 2 intrinsically consistent but mutually inconsistent criterion-interpretation models. Rater 1’s scores were most consistent with the reasoning quality approach (partial credit to clinical competence independent of vignette context). Rater 2’s scores were most consistent with the context fidelity approach (near-zero scores for wrong vignette responses independent of reasoning quality). Contrary to the self-preference hypothesis, both raters placed the other higher-performing model above their own. Under rater 1, C6 (PARM reflection) was the lowest-scoring criterion across all 4 models, whereas rater 2 showed greater model-dependent variation in C6 scoring. Conclusions AI raters used in LLM-based clinical benchmarking do not behave as interchangeable scoring tools. Their scoring behavior is most consistent with model-specific criterion interpretation patterns that systematically produce different outcomes. The observed low interrater reliability requires interpretation rather than simply being ignored: it reflects structured, direction-specific disagreement concentrated in models with context-tracking failures, not random inconsistency. PARM reflection showed a notable yet evaluator-dependent scoring pattern that warranted further investigation, rather than being interpreted as an evaluator-independent deficit.

items.title: Systemwide adoption patterns of ambient AI scribe technology in an integrated academic health system
items.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes may reduce documentation burden, but little is known about their adoption during enterprise-scale ambulatory rollout. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of 2901 ambulatory clinicians at an integrated academic health system using linked electronic health record and vendor usage data from December 2024 through May 2025. Clinician adoption was defined as any use during the study period, and monthly visit-level uptake as the proportion of eligible ambulatory visits in which the ambient AI scribe was used. Adoption and uptake varied substantially across practice settings, specialties, and clinician types. Clinician-level adoption was highest in community internal medicine (67%), community general pediatrics (69%), and academic neurology (53%), and lowest in academic general surgery (16%), obstetrics and gynecology (18%), and psychiatry (19%). Community attending physicians and advanced practice providers showed marked increases in median visit-level uptake, reaching approximately 80%-90% in some groups by May 2025. Distinct longitudinal patterns included slow and steady adoption, early use followed by discontinuation, transient use, and late adoption. These findings suggest that implementation support and evaluation strategies should be tailored to local practice context rather than applied uniformly across a health system.

items.title: Talking or typing? How GenAI modality, product type, and multitasking shape recommendation response behaviour
items.abstract: Purpose This research aims to explore how generative AI (GenAI) recommendation modality (text vs voice) influences consumer recommendation adoption and how this effect further interacts with product type (search vs experience), processing fluency and multitasking to shape consumers’ behavioural responses to recommendations. Given that GenAI recommendation systems increasingly support interactive consumer decision-making, the authors examine modality as a key design feature shaping how GenAI-generated recommendations are delivered to consumers. Design/methodology/approach Across five studies, the authors examine how GenAI recommendation modality influences consumers’ recommendation adoption. The preliminary field study uses actual customer interactions in a natural commercial environment to establish the practical relevance of the phenomenon. Study 1 replicates the core modality effect in a controlled Chinese experiment. Study 2 examines the moderating role of product type. Studies 3 and 4 investigate processing fluency and multitasking as the underlying mechanism and boundary condition, using behavioural measures across all studies. Findings The findings demonstrate that GenAI recommendation modality affects consumers’ recommendation adoption, with text-based recommendations outperforming voice-based recommendations. The modality also interacts with product type and this effect is mediated by processing fluency: text-based recommendations elicit stronger behavioural responses for search products, whereas voice-based recommendations are more effective for experience products. Multitasking further moderates this pattern, favouring voice-based recommendations under high cognitive load across product types. Research limitations/implications The findings are based on controlled experimental settings and future work could examine additional contextual or individual-level moderators to enhance external validity. Practical implications Marketers should tailor GenAI recommendation modalities based on product type and anticipated multitasking environments. Text-based interactions are more suitable for detail-oriented search products, whereas voice-based interactions better suit experience products and multitasking contexts. Originality/value This research contributes to the GenAI literature by identifying recommendation modality as a critical yet understudied design feature of GenAI recommendation systems. The findings show that recommendation modality plays a central role in shaping consumer responses to GenAI-generated recommendations and extend processing fluency theory and task–technology fit by integrating product type and multitasking as key boundary conditions.
